title: Armed nanobodies as anti-infectives and anti-tumor agents
text:
The administration in vivo of fusion proteins composed of an anti-immunoglobulin light chain nanobody,
VHHkappa, and a nanobody that recognizes virus-infected cells or tumor cells results in the recruitment to the
targeted cell of polyclonal immunoglobulins of all isotypes and of indeterminate specificity. In vivo administration
of such fusions eliminates these targeted cells, including tumors. We will define in detail the underlying
mechanisms of action and include cytotoxic drugs to further improve the efficacy of such fusions.

title: Harnessing novel machine learning approaches for behavioral segmentation and brain signal integration in humanized models of Alzheimer's disease
text:
Recent advances in computer vision and machine learning (ML), including pose estimation and behavioral
segmentation, offer unprecedented improvements for behavioral phenotyping and are uniquely suited to assess
the subtle cognitive changes in the recently-developed humanized Alzheimer’s disease (AD) models generated
by the NIH (MODEL-AD). We propose to validate and further develop our multi-scale and multi-modal ML
platforms for comprehensive behavioral phenotyping of spontaneous behavior, cognitive functions, and
therapeutic interventions in newly developed AD KI mice.

title: The Neural Circuit Basis of Olfactory Navigation in Adult Drosophila
text:
How the brain uses odor cues to find food is not well understood. In this project we will investigate the
function of an ancient navigation center called the fan-shaped body in transforming odor cues into
navigational movements. This project will help us understand how brain circuits are organized to allow
for goal-directed movements.

title: The Role of Corticolimbic Circuits in Maternal Behavior
text:
Corticolimbic circuits play an important role in maternal care, threat and stress responses postpartum, but it is
still unknown which neuronal mechanisms connect corticolimbic circuits with core maternal circuits. To this
end, we will determine the role of neuroplasticity in a specific corticolimbic circuit, using a multidisciplinary
approach that uniquely positions us to address these questions. It will have a significant positive impact on our
mechanistic understanding of the neurobiology of the motherhood and may contribute to the design of new
therapeutic approaches to prevent and decrease the incidence of mental states with similar neural
mechanisms, improving well-being of mothers and their offspring.

title: "Understanding the role of arginine metabolism in antibiotic treatment failure during Staphylococcus aureus infections."
text:
Staphylococcus aureus is a leading cause of many common infections among Veterans and is associated with
roughly one out of every 50 admissions to a VA hospital. Furthermore, S. aureus is the most common bacterial
cause of mortality in the United States. These high rates of mortality are driven by elevated rates of antibiotic
treatment failure, which exceeds 15% for some S. aureus infections. Despite the clinical significance of antibiotic
tolerance, the mechanisms by which it occurs are poorly understood. Depletion of arginine leads to an increase
in antibiotic tolerance in mature S. aureus communities. Using a combination of in vitro experiments, tissue
culture, in vivo mouse infection models, and advanced imaging mass spectroscopy, I will test the hypothesis that
S. aureus is able to regulate the level of arginine to promote its own survival and persistence in the presence of
antibiotics and the innate immune system.

title: Methods for Unraveling the Impact of Dietary Xenobiotics on COPD Exacerbations with Multi-Dimensional Networks
text:
Despite growing evidence of nutrition’s role in modulating the risk of COPD and COPD-related
manifestations, we lack a mechanistic understanding of how dietary chemicals may synergistically
exert their influence. Here, we develop a new set of machine learning and network science-based
methods specifically designed to explore the impact of small molecules directly derived from food
digestion, absorption, and related metabolism (dietary xenobiotics) on COPD exacerbation
frequency and severity. These methods will help identify tailored interventions, combining
pharmacological and dietary approaches, to mitigate lung disease through the use of Precision
Nutrition.

title: Genome structure, transcription and packaging of dsRNA viruses
text: Viruses in the Reoviridae family infect a wide range of hosts, including animals, plants, fungi, and bacteria; within this family, rotaviruses cause 450,000 deaths worldwide each year, and BTV kills livestock, with devastating economic and social consequences. The proposed structural and functional studies focus on BTV and CPV to provide structural answers to fundamental questions of replication of these and other dsRNA viruses. The results will provide profound insight into the structural basis of dsRNA virus spread and inform rational development of anti-viral drugs and vaccines against these and other viruses.

title: Combination Therapy with Semaglutide and Anti-Amyloid Antibodies for Alzheimers Disease
text:
Recent FDA conditional approvals of two anti-amyloid antibody treatments for early-stage Alzheimer’s disease
provide the first disease-modifying treatments to date, albeit with modest-to-moderate slowing of cognitive
decline and vascular side effects. Here, we will test the efficacy of a Glucagon-Like Peptide 1 Receptor (GLP-
1R) agonist, semaglutide, a drug with strong anti-inflammatory, neuroprotective and pro-vascular health effects
that is FDA approved for type 2 diabetes and obesity, both alone and in combination with anti-amyloid antibodies
in mouse models of Alzheimer’s disease. We hypothesize that the combination therapy will enhance the efficacy
beyond that of either treatment alone, and attenuate the vascular side effects seen with anti-amyloid antibodies.

title: The Impact of Myosin-Binding Protein C on Myosin Mobility and Proteostasis.
text:
Cardiac muscle myosin molecules are organized within large macromolecular complexes, yet recent data
suggest that individual molecules are quickly exchanged within these complexes to maintain cellular balance.
Preliminary findings indicate that myosin-binding protein C (MyBP-C) plays a crucial role in regulating this
exchange, and its absence in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy disrupts complex stability and contractile function.
This project aims to uncover the mechanisms by which MyBP-C governs these processes and to evaluate the
impact of two distinct therapeutic approaches in correcting these dysfunctions.

title: Synergistic Regulation of Germline Development by PUFs and small RNAs
text:
Germ granules are assemblies of proteins and RNAs essential for animal reproduction, supporting the
development and function of germ cells. Leveraging the powerful genetic tools available in C. elegans, we will
define the mechanisms mediating co-regulation of gene expression and germ cell development by RNA-binding
proteins and small RNA pathways localized in germ granules. Ultimately, this work will improve our
understanding of the genetic causes of germ cell dysfunction underlying human infertility and the misregulation
of germ-cell-specific pathways implicated in cancer.

title: Bioimaging Resource Core
text: The Bioimaging Resource Core (BRC) is a critical component of the Wake Forest Older Americans Independence Center (WF OAIC). It provides leadership, scientific expertise, and instrumental support in quantitative imaging, including CT, MRI, DXA, PET, and ultrasound, critical to the WF OAIC’s research theme: Integrating pathways affecting physical function for new approaches to disability treatment and prevention. The BRC is well integrated with other OAIC cores and supports investigators’ use of imaging to characterize body and brain structure and function. In the present cycle, the BRC facilitated 4 OAIC scholars, 8 pilot and development projects, contributed to 80 original papers, and 19 new NIH awards, including 5 to early-career investigators. The BRC and the WF OAIC Biostatistics and Research Information Systems Core partnered with the WF Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center to harmonize storage, processing, archiving, and access of imaging data for body and brain to facilitate research integrating the biology of aging and mobility with brain health. The BRC also developed, validated, and implemented innovative image acquisition and analysis methods for muscle, fat, bone, and brain phenotypes. The Specific Aims of the BRC for the new cycle are to: 1) Support pilot, development, and externally-funded research projects with quantitative imaging phenotypes for use in observational and intervention research evaluating factors affecting pathways to mobility disability; 2) Develop and validate new imaging measures relevant to pathways affecting physical function. These will include trabecular and cortical bone microarchitecture acquired with a new high-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography (HR- pQCT) scanner; CT-radiomics of muscle, fat, and bone; “CT-body-age” and “MRI-brain-age” and functional brain network metrics associated with mobility; and 3) Apply imaging techniques in support of WF OAIC programmatic goals by: training researchers focused on disability treatment and prevention to integrate imaging methods; collaborating with other OAIC cores to develop multidisciplinary, translational projects; and disseminating data and methods for use by the national research community. In the first year of the next cycle, BRC will support 16 studies including 1 BRC-led research Development Project, 2 Pilot studies (1 led by a REC Scholar), and 13 Externally-funded studies. The BRC will be led by three highly experienced, independently successful investigators: Leon Lenchik, MD, Christina Hugenschmidt, PhD and Ashley Weaver, PhD. They have complementary skills and expertise and strong records of collaborative scientific and administrative achievements. They will ensure the achievement of the BRC goals and its contributions to the overall success of the WF OAIC.

title: Computational Molecular & Functional Imaging Training (CMFIT) Program
text:
The Computational, Molecular & Functional Imaging Training (CMFIT) Program will address the need for
proficient investigators with a profound grasp of the medical/biomedical problems to be solved coupled with
robust quantitative skills essential for academic careers and highly desired by various industries. CMFIT will
select doctoral candidates after their first year of graduate school to join the program and provide them with two
years of interdisciplinary research training in biomedical imaging, and academic and professional development.

title: Multi-cancer Early Detection
text:
In the United States, cancer is the leading cause of death for persons under 80 years of age. Screening of
persons without cancer symptoms is only practiced for colorectal, breast, cervical and lung cancer and saves
lives. This proposal will address key questions surrounding a new cancer screening concept, the multi-cancer
detection test which might facilitate screening for additional cancer types by measuring cancer cell-free DNA to
detect multiple cancer types from a single venous blood draw.

title: Analysis of the Metabolic Capabilities of Prokaryotic Cells
text:
The goal of the proposed work is to understand the molecular underpinnings of fundamental
metabolic and physiologic processes in microbial cells, especially in human pathogens, with the
goal of providing potential therapeutic targets to treat human disease.

title: Neuronal mechanisms of deep brain stimulation for psychiatric disorders
text:
Brain stimulation techniques, including deep brain stimulation, have yielded major breakthroughs in the treatment of
otherwise untreatable mental illnesses. Stimulation technologies advance rapidly but how they affect the activity of
individual neurons and neuronal circuits distributed throughout the brain, and how this activity relates to symptoms of
mental illness remains poorly understood. The goal of this proposal is to study acute and chronic brain-wide effects of deep
brain stimulation on single-neuron activity during compulsive behaviors in mice and compare these to electrical signals in
brains of patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder to improve how brain stimulation protocols can be tailored to
symptoms.

title: Information encoding by spatiotemporal patterns of dopamine release
text:
Midbrain dopamine (DA) neurons were classically thought to homogeneously encode reward prediction errors,
but recent evidence has demonstrated that they also encode other behavioral variables, including value-neutral
sensory prediction errors. Reconciling foundational concepts and these recent findings, as well as with what is
known about the cellular properties and circuit connectivity of DA neurons, is currently one of the key challenges
in the field. This project combines a validated odor-guided choice task with a new DA imaging approach
developed by the candidate, as well as drug self-administration, chemogenetic, and gene editing methods, to
test the hypothesis that spatiotemporal patterns of DA release encode a multi-factorial prediction-error teaching
signal, and that the informational components of this signal are vulnerable to pathophysiological challenges,
depend on the contribution of upstream cortical circuits, and are shaped by specific biophysical properties of DA
neurons.

title: Live Imaging of Skin Regeneration
text:
Stem cells have the unique ability to replenish both themselves and the specialized cell types of our organs.
Dysregulation of this balance leads to diverse diseases, such as fibrosis and cancer, that lack effective
treatments. We use novel microscopy approaches to study this balance in the skin in live animals, which allows
us to discover previously unknown mechanisms that sustain our organs, how these mechanisms go awry in
disease, and potential therapeutic strategies to restore balance.

title: Measurement of Care Needs in Youth with VST Congenital Conditions
text: This project addresses the interdisciplinary care and self-report needs of youth with variations in sex traits (VST), also known as differences of sex development. By recruiting a diagnostically representative sample of youth and emerging adults with VST, and developing, calibrating, and validating a self-report tool for youth with VST, this psychometric initiative will provide young people greater support in communicating regarding their care—care which often involves irreversible medical decision-making during childhood and adolescence with life-long ramifications for well-being, sexual and urological function, and psychosocial health. The resulting measure will also identify and characterize VST health-related distress to inform patient-centered interdisciplinary clinical care practices and will examine variations in VST outcomes to inform interdisciplinary care models.

title: Revealing Metastatic Tumor Microenvironmental Mechanisms in Osteosarcoma to Develop Novel Therapeutic Approaches
text:
Osteosarcoma is a devastating cancer with very poor outcomes if metastasis takes
place. By studying how this cancer spreads we are finding opportunities to develop
novel therapies that could allow more children with this disease to live. Further, the
mechanisms that underly how this disease works seem to be shared across other types
of cancer and so our work could have broad implications and improve the outlook for
many patients.

title: Inflammatory mechanisms of dysbiosis in laryngeal glottic stenosis
text:
The research proposed in this application will investigate the role of dysbiosis-mediated immune activation in
glottic wound healing following intubation injury, using human samples and a novel mouse model. This
proposal also investigates microbiome modulation as an innovative approach to reduce chronic immune
activation and prevent glottic scar.
